Fresh carrots have a sweet, earthy flavour rarely matched by shop-bought roots. Establishment can be tricky: germination is slow and slugs attack seedlings. Deep, fine, stone-free soil helps roots grow straight and tender; light soil or compost-filled no-dig beds can work well. Sow short successions for early-summer to autumn harvests. Looking after the crop
Weed seedlings carefully; avoid hoeing close to established roots or loosening their soil.

Care & harvest · Outdoor tomato
Looking after the crop
Support cordons; tie about every 12 in. and remove side shoots around 1 in. long. Stop above the last useful truss by late summer. Remove yellow leaves sparingly; keep healthy foliage. Bushes normally need no side-shooting or stopping.
Water roots steadily; feed organically as fruit develops. Keep low fruit off wet soil. Ventilate cloches in warmth: they reduce rain on leaves; fleece does not prevent blight. Check for blight.
Harvesting & storage
Pick fully coloured fruit gently; keep stalks where possible, avoid skin damage and use promptly. Tall types often crop August–October; bushes July–September. DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Fresh carrots have a sweet, earthy flavour rarely matched by shop-bought roots. Establishment can be tricky: germination is slow and slugs attack seedlings. Tomato, Outdoor.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Outdoor tomatoes have plenty of flavour to offer, but need a warm, sunny, sheltered site and a variety suited to British summers. Choose plants labelled for outdoor cultivation; in cooler areas, cloches or other protection can make a crop more reliable. Tall cordon tomatoes need staking, side-shooting and stopping near the end of the season so existing fruit can ripen. Bush or determinate tomatoes need less pruning and can be grown under cloches or in containers. Keep low fruit clear of the ground where practical and check for slugs and blight.

Recommended varieties
CORDON
Outdoor Girl

An early cordon tomato suited to outdoor growing. Provide support and remove sideshoots as for other cordon varieties.

CORDON
Gardener's Delight

A familiar cordon tomato with small red fruits. A useful outdoor choice in a warm, sheltered position.

CORDON
Crimson Crush F1

A cordon tomato bred for outdoor growing with strong late-blight resistance. Produces large red fruits for slicing and cooking.

CORDON
Sungold F1

A sweet orange cherry tomato for a sunny, sheltered outdoor site. Grow as a supported cordon and pick ripe fruits promptly.

BUSH
Red Alert

An early bush tomato with small red fruits. Useful where compact plants are preferred to tall, trained cordons.

Key risks
Blight

Blight causes rapidly spreading brown leaf and stem lesions and fruit decay in damp weather.

Blossom end rot

A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates.

Slugs

Slugs chew low-hanging fruit, particularly on bush plants.

Split fruit

Ripe fruit may split after irregular watering or rain following dry soil.

Sow under cover

Growing guide · Tomato, Outdoor
FRUITING CROPS

FRUITING CROPS
Care & harvest · Outdoor tomato
Looking after the crop
Support cordons; tie about every 30 cm and remove side shoots around 2.5 cm long. Stop above the last useful truss by late summer. Remove yellow leaves sparingly; keep healthy foliage. Bushes normally need no side-shooting or stopping.
Water roots steadily; feed organically as fruit develops. Keep low fruit off wet soil. Ventilate cloches in warmth: they reduce rain on leaves; fleece does not prevent blight. Check for blight.
Harvesting & storage
Pick fully coloured fruit gently; keep stalks where possible, avoid skin damage and use promptly. Tall types often crop August–October; bushes July–September. Bring sound unripe fruit indoors at season’s end. Ripen in shallow trays at room temperature; check for rot. A ripe apple or banana nearby helps. Use tested bottling or green-tomato chutney recipes.
Pests & diseases
Problem · what to look for	What to do
Blight — Brown dying leaves; dark fruit rot.	Remove infected plants; keep foliage dry where practical.
Blossom end rot — Dark leathery patch at fruit base.	Keep roots evenly moist, especially as fruit swells.
Slugs — Low fruit is chewed or hollowed.	Keep fruit off soil; check and hand-pick near vulnerable plants.
Split fruit — Fruit cracks after rain or uneven watering.	Keep root moisture steady and mulch.
Aphids — Colonies on young growth.	Tolerate light colonies; squash damaging ones; encourage predators.
Grey mould (Botrytis) — Grey mould on damaged stems or fruit.	Remove infected tissue and dead material; ventilate.
Virus — Leaves mottled and distorted; plants stunted.	Remove affected plants; clean hands/tools; monitor aphids.
Blossom drop — Flowers wither and fall without setting.	Water steadily; ventilate in heat; gently tap trusses.
Cutworms — Young stems are severed near soil level.	Protect seedlings with collars; inspect nearby soil.
Final tips

Check beneath bush foliage often: ripe fruit and slug damage are easily missed.

Stop tall plants in time for the local season; leave two leaves above the final truss.

DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Potatoes give heavy crops from small plots; check old grassland for wireworms. Plant seed tubers, not true seed, and keep new tubers covered: light makes them green and poisonous. Eat first/second earlies fresh. Maincrops yield and store better, but need more space and face more blight. Give rich soil and moisture; guard frost-tender leaves. Lift gently; store maincrops cool, dark and frost-free.

Key risks
Blight

Potato blight spreads rapidly in warm, wet weather, causing brown foliage lesions, collapse and potentially tuber decay.

Slugs

Slugs tunnel into tubers, particularly in damp soil or beneath covers and mulches.

Scab

Common scab causes corky skin patches and is favoured by dry conditions as tubers form, particularly in alkaline soil.

Eelworm

Potato cyst nematodes can build up where potatoes are grown repeatedly.

Choose the crop for your needs.

Earlies give fresh new potatoes; maincrops give larger storage harvests.

Soil & preparation
Fertile, slightly acid soil with rotted compost/manure. Rotate; avoid liming.

Prepare seed potatoes 

Use healthy certified seed potatoes. Chitting means letting them sprout before planting: stand them with the eyes upwards in a cool, light, frost-free place. It is most useful for first earlies.

Plant in the ground 

Early planting needs a mild or protected site. Make trenches about 15 cm deep, or use individual holes. This is the trench depth, not 15 cm of soil above each tuber. Set tubers at the base with sprouts upwards, cover gently and water well. Follow the early/maincrop spacings in Quick Facts; earth up as the stems grow to keep developing tubers covered. Protect emerging shoots from frost.

Alternative: under mulch 

Set tubers on the soil surface and cover with a thick mulch that excludes light. Keep topping it up so tubers cannot turn green, and check for slugs.

Alternative: containers 

Use a large container with drainage. Start tubers in a shallow layer of compost, cover them and add more compost as the stems grow. Keep tubers covered and water regularly.

Growing guide · Potato
ROOT CROPS

ROOT CROPS
Care & harvest · Potato
Looking after the crop
Protect shoots from frost. Earth up or mulch before tubers are exposed; weed carefully and water as tubers swell, especially in pots.
If blight becomes established, remove affected haulm and debris. Where conditions permit, wait about two weeks before lifting; use sound tubers promptly.
Harvesting & storage
Test-lift earlies at a useful size; flowering alone is unreliable. Use fresh. Fork storage crops after haulm dies, before severe frost. Collect every tuber, including tiny ones, to reduce volunteers and disease carry-over.
Dry briefly out of strong light. Store sound, dry tubers cool, dark and frost-free in breathable jute, canvas or paper sacks, never sealed plastic. Use sound damaged tubers first; discard rot.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Blight	Brown collapsing foliage; tubers may rot.	Remove affected haulm; allow skins to set before lifting where possible.
Slugs	Deep tunnels spoil tubers.	Avoid slug refuges; lift mature crops promptly.
Scab	Corky skin patches on tubers.	Avoid liming; keep soil moist as tubers form.
Eelworm	Stunted patches; cysts on roots.	Rotate; use suitable resistant varieties after diagnosis.
Frost	Young foliage blackens.	Cover shoots before frost; unfrozen plants may regrow.
Storage rots	Tubers soften or decay in store.	Store only sound dry tubers; inspect and remove rot.
Blackleg	Stem bases blacken; leaves wilt.	Remove affected plants; use healthy certified seed.
Wireworm	Narrow tunnels riddle tubers.	Avoid infested ground; remove larvae and lift promptly.
Wart disease	Cauliflower-like growths around eyes.	Do not move soil or tubers; report for official diagnosis.
Colorado beetle	Striped yellow beetles or spotted larvae.	Contain securely, photograph and report; do not release.
Final tips

Check mulch/ridges often. Keep tubers covered; never eat green ones.

Check stores often; remove soft or rotten tubers to stop decay.
